title: 3-5-7 Rule for Day Trading in 2026
description: Learn the 3-5-7 rule for day trading: risk 3% per trade, cap total risk at 5% and aim for winners that make 7%. Clear examples and the mistakes that break it.
alt: Trader applying strict risk management rules with 3-5-7 strategy on trading charts

content.text: Trading accounts rarely die from one catastrophic trade. A more common pattern is a string of small losses, each a little bigger than the last, taken in a hurry with no limits. Picture eight trades in one morning, each risking a bit more than the one before, and an account down close to a fifth before the trader has noticed what is happening. The cause isn't bad luck. It's the absence of rules. The 3-5-7 rule is a simple set of limits designed to prevent exactly that.
What the 3-5-7 Rule Actually Is
The 3-5-7 rule is a risk management rule of thumb, not an official standard, and you'll find slightly different versions online. The most common one has three parts:

items: 3% rule: never risk more than 3% of your total trading capital on a single trade.
5% rule: keep the total risk across all open positions under 5% of your capital.
7% target: aim for winning trades that make at least 7% of your capital.

content.text: Some versions describe the 7 as a 7:1 reward-to-risk ratio instead. That's a far higher bar than most traders reach consistently, so this guide uses the more common profit-target version. With 3% at risk and a 7% target, the reward is a little over twice the risk (about 2.3 to 1).
The 3% Rule: Your Single-Trade Limit

You will be wrong often. Even skilled traders lose a large share of their trades, and what separates them from the rest is managing the losses. The 3% rule limits your loss on any single trade to 3% of your account: $300 on a $10,000 account, $600 on $20,000 and $1,500 on $50,000.
Losses are harder to recover than they look. After a 10% loss you need an 11% gain to break even, and after a 20% loss you need a 25% gain. Keeping each loss small keeps recovery realistic.

One point trips people up: the 3% is what you'd lose if your stop-loss is hit, not the size of the position. A trader with $20,000 who sets a stop 4% below entry can hold a $15,000 position and still risk only $600. Position size equals your risk amount divided by the distance to your stop. Stops aren't guaranteed either. In fast markets price can jump past them, so a real loss can end up larger than planned, which is one reason newer traders often risk 1% or 2% instead.
The 5% Rule: Your Total Exposure Cap

You can follow the 3% rule on every trade and still take far too much risk. Three open trades at 3% each means 9% of your account is at risk, and if the trades are in markets that move together, one event can hit all of them at once.

The 5% rule caps total risk across all open positions. On a $20,000 account that's $1,000, which could be two trades at $500, three at about $333, or one at $600 and one at $400. It forces you to be selective, because you can't open trade after trade without thinking about the total.
The 7% Target: Making Winners Pay for Losers

The target is what makes the maths work. If you risk 3% to make 7%, you only need to win about 3 trades in 10 to break even, before spreads and commissions: 3 ÷ (3 + 7) = 30%. Win more often than that and you make money.
Here's how that looks on a $20,000 account, risking $600 per trade and aiming for $1,400 on winners, over 20 trades:
These figures ignore trading costs, which would reduce every row. Notice that below a 30% win rate the strategy loses money even with a good target, so the edge has to be real.
A Worked Example With a $20,000 Account

items: 3% single-trade risk: $20,000 × 0.03 = $600 maximum loss on any one trade.
5% total exposure: $20,000 × 0.05 = $1,000 maximum risk across all open positions.
7% target: $20,000 × 0.07 = $1,400 profit target on a winning trade.

content.text: Now say you take three trades in a week. One hits its target for +$1,400, and two hit their stops for -$600 each. The net result is +$200. You won only one trade in three and still finished ahead. You don't need to be right often. You need your winners to be big enough to cover your losers, and that only works if you actually stick to the stops.
Why Traders Break the Rules

Because emotions are powerful. Once you're in a trade you're not thinking about rules. You're thinking about the money you could make, the loss you want to avoid and the need to be proved right. The 3-5-7 rule is as much about psychology as maths: it makes decisions in advance, when you're calm, so you don't have to make them in the heat of a losing trade.
4 Mistakes That Break the Rule

items: Moving the stop-loss. The price drops, you widen the stop because you think it will bounce, and a planned $600 loss becomes $2,000. The stop is a rule, not a suggestion.
Overtrading. Taking too many trades ignores the 5% cap. It feels like diversification but it's usually just more risk.
Chasing losses. After a bad trade, taking another immediately to win it back turns trading into gambling. If you have a bad day, close the platform and come back tomorrow.
Ignoring the target. Taking trades where the likely reward is barely bigger than the risk. At 3% risk for a 3% gain you'd need to win well over half your trades just to break even.

content.text: How the 3-5-7 Rule Compares to Other Strategies

rows: Fixed % risk, exposure cap and a profit target
Day and swing traders who value discipline
Needs patience to find setups with enough upside
Losses compound until the account can't absorb them

content.text: Your Action Plan

items: Step 1: Calculate your 3% and 5% numbers now and write them where you can see them while you trade.
Step 2: For the next 30 days, practise the rule on a demo account. Don't use real money until you've shown you can follow it.
Step 3: Journal every trade: entry, risk, target and whether you followed the rules. Review it weekly.
Step 4: If you break a rule, stop trading for the day. No exceptions.

content.text: The 3-5-7 Rule as Part of a Complete Wealth System

A risk rule helps you survive trading, but trading isn't the same as building wealth. Trading is high-risk and most people don't succeed. Building wealth is a system that starts with budgeting, moves to saving, then investing, and finally increasing your income. Trading, if it's part of your plan at all, is a small part.

If you want to build wealth the right way, start with the foundation in Building Wealth From Scratch: The 5-Step System That Actually Works. It covers everything from your first emergency fund to consistent investing and extra income streams.
Final Thought

The market is indifferent to your needs, your bad day or your confidence. It just moves, and if you trade without rules it will take your money. A rule like this limits damage but doesn't create an edge, so discipline matters more than any single strategy. This article is for education only and isn't financial advice. Trading carries a high risk of loss.

faq.question: What is the 3-5-7 rule in day trading?
faq.answer: A risk management rule of thumb: risk no more than 3% of your account on any one trade, keep total risk across open trades under 5%, and aim for winners that make at least 7% of your capital. Versions vary, so check how a source defines the 7.

faq.question: Why is the 3-5-7 rule so effective?
faq.answer: It shifts the focus from winning to risk management. By capping losses and requiring winners that are larger than losers, a trader can be profitable with a win rate below 50%. With 3% risk and a 7% target the break-even win rate is about 30% before costs.

faq.question: Can I use the 3-5-7 rule with a small account?
faq.answer: Yes, but execution is harder. With a $500 account, 3% is $15, which requires very small position sizes or micro lots, and spreads take a bigger share. The principle scales, but small accounts leave little room for error.

faq.question: What happens if I break the 3-5-7 rule?
faq.answer: You risk losing more than you planned, and one bad trade can wipe out weeks of gains. If you break it, stop trading for the day, review what happened and restart with the rules the next day.

faq.question: Is the 3-5-7 rule only for day trading?
faq.answer: No. It can be applied to swing trading and position trading as well. The stops may be wider, but the 3% and 5% limits still work as caps on risk.

final_advice.text: Rules won't make a weak strategy profitable, but they keep you in the game long enough to find out whether yours works. Set your limits before you place a trade, write them down and treat them as non-negotiable.
